metric_identity.metric_name: AI Energy & Data Center Power Demand
metric_identity.source_report: IEA 'Energy and AI' report (October 2025); Goldman Sachs Research 'Data Center Power Demand: The 6 Ps' (September 2025); LBNL '2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report' (December 2024); Pew Research Center analysis (October 2025)
metric_identity.publication_date: October 2025 (IEA Energy and AI); September 2025 (Goldman Sachs); December 2024 (LBNL)
metric_identity.methodology_notes: The IEA Energy and AI report (October 2025) is the primary authoritative source. IEA methodology uses near-term industry projections for server shipments as the key input, modeling both accelerated servers (AI-optimized, growing 30% annually) and conventional servers (growing 9% annually). The IEA Base Case projects global data center electricity consumption at ~415 TWh in 2024, doubling to ~945 TWh by 2030. For the US specifically, the LBNL 2024 report estimated 176 TWh by 2023 (4.4% of US electricity), while IEA estimates 183 TWh for 2024 (4%+ of US electricity). The IEA uses multiple scenarios (Base Case, High Efficiency, and faster-growth variants) to account for uncertainty. Goldman Sachs uses a bottom-up model based on data center capacity (GW), utilization rates, and power usage effectiveness (PUE), projecting 165% growth in global data center power demand by 2030 vs. 2023. McKinsey projects a more aggressive 22.3% CAGR for US data centers, reaching 606 TWh by 2030.

metric_value.value: Global data center electricity: ~415 TWh in 2024 (~1.5% of global electricity). US data centers: 183 TWh in 2024 (4%+ of US electricity). AI's share of data center power: 5-15% in 2024, projected to reach 35-50% by 2030.
metric_value.unit: TWh (terawatt-hours) for electricity consumption; percentage of total electricity generation; GW (gigawatts) for capacity
metric_value.geographic_scope: Global, with US and China as dominant regions (together accounting for ~80% of data center electricity growth to 2030)
metric_value.comparison_baseline: Global data center electricity was approximately 240 TWh in 2020 and 340 TWh in 2022, representing roughly 73% growth from 2020 to 2024. US data center electricity was 176 TWh in 2023 (LBNL), up from approximately 130 TWh in 2020. Prior to the AI boom (2015-2020), data center electricity growth was relatively flat due to efficiency gains offsetting demand growth.

trend.year_over_year_change: Global data center electricity grew ~22% YoY from 2022 to 2024 (~340 TWh to ~415 TWh). US data center electricity grew from 176 TWh (2023) to 183 TWh (2024), ~4% YoY, but growth is accelerating sharply as new AI-optimized facilities come online. IEA projects 15% annual growth for data center electricity consumption from 2024 to 2030, more than 4x faster than total electricity consumption growth from all other sectors. Accelerated (AI) server electricity consumption is growing at 30% annually.
trend.compound_annual_growth_rate: IEA Base Case: ~15% CAGR for global data center electricity (2024-2030). Goldman Sachs: 17% CAGR for global data center capacity (2025-2028); 15% CAGR for US data centers reaching 455 TWh by 2030. McKinsey: 22.3% CAGR for US data centers reaching 606 TWh by 2030. AI-specific (accelerated servers): ~30% CAGR.
trend.forecast_value: IEA Base Case: ~945 TWh globally by 2030 (just under 3% of global electricity). US: 426 TWh by 2030 (IEA, +133% vs 2024) or 455 TWh (Goldman Sachs, up to 8% of US electricity) or 606 TWh (McKinsey). China: increases ~175 TWh (+170% vs 2024). Global data center capacity: 92 GW by 2027 (Goldman Sachs). CO2 emissions from data centers: projected to reach ~1% of global energy-related emissions by 2030. Beyond 2030: IEA projects 1,300 TWh globally by 2035.
trend.velocity_indicator: Data center electricity consumption doubling time: approximately 6 years at current growth rates (2024 to 2030). AI-specific power demand quadrupling by 2030 (IEA). US data center demand projected to triple from 2022 to 2030 (17 GW to up to 130 GW per Goldman Sachs). Single AI training run power: a frontier model training run now consumes as much electricity as 1,000+ US households use in a year.

entrepreneurial_relevance.relevance_for_entrepreneurs: The energy constraint is becoming the binding constraint on AI scaling, creating both existential risks and massive opportunities for entrepreneurs. For AI startups, energy costs are an increasingly dominant component of operational expenses: training a frontier model can cost tens of millions of dollars in compute/energy alone, and inference at scale (serving millions of users) represents a growing recurring energy cost. This creates a strong incentive for energy-efficient AI architectures, model compression, and inference optimization startups. For energy-sector entrepreneurs, data center power demand represents the fastest-growing electricity load in history, creating opportunities in: (1) power purchase agreements and energy brokering for data centers, (2) on-site generation solutions (solar+storage, natural gas, small modular nuclear reactors), (3) waste heat recovery and district heating from data centers, (4) grid infrastructure and transmission upgrades, (5) cooling technology innovation (liquid cooling, immersion cooling). The geographic dimension matters: data centers are increasingly sited based on power availability, creating economic development opportunities in regions with surplus clean energy (Nordics, Quebec, Iceland). For European entrepreneurs specifically, the EU Energy Efficiency Directive now requires data center energy and emissions reporting, creating demand for sustainability monitoring and optimization tools. The nuclear renaissance driven by AI demand (Microsoft-Constellation TMI restart, Google-Kairos 500MW SMR deal) opens opportunities in nuclear supply chain and services startups.
entrepreneurial_relevance.actionable_insight: AI startups should factor energy costs into unit economics from day one and consider geographic arbitrage (locating compute in regions with cheap, clean power). Build products that reduce AI energy intensity: model distillation tools, inference optimization platforms, efficient architecture search, and carbon-aware scheduling. Energy entrepreneurs should target the data center power supply chain: 6+ GW of new capacity is being built in the US alone (Stargate), and the EU's AI Gigafactories will need dedicated power infrastructure. Cooling technology is a near-term opportunity as AI chips push thermal density limits. Sustainability reporting tools for data center operators are a regulatory-driven growth market in the EU.

confidence.cross_reference: The 415 TWh global figure and 945 TWh 2030 projection are from the IEA's October 2025 'Energy and AI' report, confirmed by S&P Global, Nature, Scientific American, Carbon Brief, and Data Center Dynamics. The US 183 TWh figure is cited by IEA and confirmed by Pew Research Center (October 2025). The LBNL 2024 report (December 2024) independently estimated 176 TWh for US data centers in 2023, consistent with the IEA's 183 TWh for 2024 after accounting for growth. Goldman Sachs Research (September 2025) projects 165% growth by 2030, broadly consistent with IEA's doubling estimate. McKinsey's 22.3% CAGR is the most aggressive major-institution estimate but represents the high end of a credible range. The 4%+ US electricity share is confirmed across IEA, LBNL, Pew Research, and DOE sources.
confidence.caveats: Significant uncertainty in forecasts due to: (1) AI adoption rates may accelerate or decelerate unpredictably (DeepSeek-style efficiency breakthroughs could reduce demand growth); (2) energy efficiency improvements (PUE, chip efficiency, model optimization) could partially offset demand growth; (3) IEA notes that actual data center electricity consumption is notoriously difficult to measure due to inconsistent reporting by operators; (4) the 415 TWh global figure is an IEA estimate, not a directly measured value; (5) forecasts assume continued GPU/accelerator scaling following current trajectories, but supply chain constraints or policy changes could alter the path; (6) the CO2 impact depends heavily on the energy mix powering data centers, which varies dramatically by region (56% fossil fuels in the US vs. near-100% renewable in some Nordic facilities); (7) water consumption for cooling is a parallel concern not captured in electricity figures alone.
